extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent practitioners, and applicants (patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing whether claimed inventions satisfy subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the USPTO two-step (Step 1; Steps 2A/2B) framework, including the two-prong 'directed to' inquiry and Markedly Different Characteristics analysis for nature-based products. Covers considerations and examples across biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, diagnostics, business methods, and software.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Statutory categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention must be to a statutory category: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter (MPEP 2106.03).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP 2106.03 explains how courts have defined the four categories, provides examples of subject matter that doesn’t fall within any category (e.g., software per se, signals per se, and human organisms), and provides guidance on how to evaluate whether the claimed invention is to one of the four statutory categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed to — two-prong inquiry (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Directed to" in Step 2A is a two-prong inquiry: Prong One — evaluate whether the claim recites a judicial exception; Prong Two — evaluate whether the claim recites additional elements that integrate the exception into a practical application of the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prong One asks whether the claim recites an abstract idea, law of nature/natural principle, or natural phenomenon/product of nature. Prong Two asks whether additional elements integrate that exception into a practical application, using considerations from case law (e.g., insignificant extra-solution activity, particular treatment or prophylaxis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — Judicial exceptions (identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites a judicial exception: abstract ideas; laws of nature/natural principles; or natural phenomena/products of nature (MPEP 2106.04).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners determine if claim limitations fall into one or more of these exception categories (see separate guidance for each grouping). Examples in the MPEP illustrate claims that do and do not recite these exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract ideas — three groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideas are evaluated by whether claim limitations fall within at least one of three groupings: mathematical concepts; mental processes; and certain methods of organizing human activity (MPEP 2106.04(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples identify claims that do not recite abstract ideas; examiners should map claim limitations to these groupings (e.g., arithmetic operations as 'mathematical concepts'; steps performable in the human mind as 'mental processes').

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of nature — Markedly Different Characteristics (MDC) analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: For nature-based products, use the Markedly Different Characteristics (MDC) analysis to determine whether a claim limitation is a 'product of nature' exception (MPEP 2106.04(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MDC can be shown by structural changes (Examples 16, 28, 30) or changes in function resulting from combinations (Examples 17, 28, 30, 44) — e.g., changes in rate of cell growth, immunogenic effect, taste, glycemic control. If the claimed product is not markedly different from the natural product, it is a product-of-nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — Integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the additional elements in the claim integrate the judicial exception into a practical application (MPEP 2106.04(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integration requires the additional element(s) to apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the exception so that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the exception. Prong Two uses court considerations such as 'insignificant extra-solution activity' and 'particular treatment or prophylaxis' to evaluate integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity and mere instructions to apply the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that are mere data-gathering steps, insignificant extra-solution activity, or high-level instructions to apply the exception do not integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'obtaining' or 'detecting' steps that are routine data-gathering; administering a treatment recited at high generality (mere instruction). Such additional elements are treated as insignificant or as mere instructions and do not confer eligibility under Step 2A Prong Two or Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: Significantly more / Inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine whether the additional elements in the claim amount to 'significantly more' — i.e., whether they provide an inventive concept beyond the judicial exception (MPEP 2106.05).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 2B uses considerations from case law including 'improvements to the functioning of a computer/other technology' and whether elements are 'well-understood, routine, conventional activity' (further explained in MPEP 2106.05(a)-(h)). Eligibility requires that additional elements amount to an inventive concept, individually or in combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well‑understood, routine, conventional activity (negative indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: If additional elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional activities, they do not supply the inventive concept needed to make the claim eligible under Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use of conventional immunoassays, conventional autoradiography, or routine reagent use — when the claimed additional steps are routine in the field, they are treated as not providing 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to technology or functioning (positive indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim elements that improve the functioning of a computer or other technology can indicate 'significantly more' and support eligibility under Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and the MPEP recognize technological improvements as a basis for finding an inventive concept; examiners should evaluate whether additional elements improve how a technology operates or solve a technological problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconventional or non-routine steps/reagents/techniques can add an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of unconventional reagents, non-routine techniques, or steps not shown to be routine in the art can be treated as more than mere instructions and can provide an inventive concept (examples: porcine antibodies; scanning near-field optical microscopy (SNOM)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is no evidence that a reagent or technique was routinely or conventionally used for the claimed purpose, that element may be an unconventional step that is more than mere instructions to apply the exception and can render the claim eligible (as shown in Example 29 claim 3 and Example 31 claim 70).
